x1ygcdtj.author: Plato
x1ygcdtj.label: Pregnant in body and in soul
x1ygcdtj.translation: I mean to say, that all men are bringing to the birth in their bodies and in their souls. There is a certain age at which human nature is desirous of procreation--procreation which must be in beauty and not in deformity; ... But souls which are pregnant--for there certainly are men who are more creative in their souls than in their bodies--conceive that which is proper for the soul to conceive or contain. And what are these conceptions?--wisdom and virtue in general.
x1ygcdtj.reading: Humans are pregnant in body but even more in soul, and the soul gestates logos and virtue, that is, awakening of consciousness. She makes this the second stage of the soul's second birth, the κυοφορία, and links it to Socrates the midwife of the Theaetetus.

xt5zovt.author: Orphic tradition
xt5zovt.ref: Orphic Hymn 77 to Mnemosyne (Taylor's no. LXXVI)
xt5zovt.label: Memory joins soul to intellect
xt5zovt.translation: THE consort I invoke of Jove divine, / Source of the holy, sweetly-speaking Nine; / Free from th' oblivion of the fallen mind, / By whom the soul with intellect is join'd: / Reason's increase, and thought to thee belong, / All-powerful, pleasant, vigilant, and strong: / 'Tis thine, to waken from lethargic rest / All thoughts deposited within the breast; / And nought neglecting, vigorous to excite / The mental eye from dark oblivion's night. / Come, blessed power, thy mystic's mem'ry wake / To holy rites, and Lethe's fetters break.
xt5zovt.translator: Thomas Taylor, The Mystical Initiations; or, Hymns of Orpheus (1792)
xt5zovt.reading: She quotes a line on mind dwelling with souls (νοῦν ψυχαῖσι σύνοικον), which her notes mark as caption-garbled and probably from this hymn (uncertain). Mnemosyne is the soul's memory of its own nature: incense (θυμίαμα) "reminds" (θυμίζει) us, and Greeks must drink again the water of Mnemosyne from Homer's spring.

xv7wzb8.author: Plato
xv7wzb8.label: The soul plunged into a river; what sensation is
xv7wzb8.translation: and fastening the courses of the immortal soul in a body which was in a state of perpetual influx and efflux. Now these courses, detained as in a vast river, neither overcame nor were overcome; ... when the body of any one met and came into collision with some external fire, or with the solid earth or the gliding waters, or was caught in the tempest borne on the air, and the motions produced by any of these impulses were carried through the body to the soul. All such motions have consequently received the general name of 'sensations,' which they still retain.
xv7wzb8.reading: The body enters the soul, not the soul the body: it is a porous seat of inflow and outflow, always in exchange with Heraclitus' river. Immersion in that river is the soul's "first baptism", and sensation is the moment the river's pulses reach the soul's circles, so it is the mind that senses, not the body.
